subsubtopic: CALL FOR CONSULTATION WITH LEASEHOLDERS IN WESTERN PARKS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. A notice from the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) appeared in The Globe and Mail on Saturday, November 8, 1980, addressed to the cottage and home leaseholders in Yoho, Banff, Jasper, Waterton Lakes, Prince Albert and Riding Mountain national parks, all located in western Canada. Inasmuch as the announcement continues the harassment of western Canadians using these parks, harassment which has included attempts to cancel arbitrarily federal leases which now take the form of sudden exorbitant land rental increases up to 1,400 per cent, creating hardships on pioneers and senior citizens in particular, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer):
That the Minister of the Environment announce immediately that he will consult, as originally promised, with leaseholders in the western national parks in an effort to arrive at a fair and equitable increase, thereby easing the growing feeling of alienation in the west arising from the many arbitrary actions of the Government of Canada.

SITE FOR METHANE TERMINAL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
November 12, 1980

Last week, I visited Gros-Cacouna, the site which had been originally proposed for the LNG methane terminal for the Arctic pilot project near Riviere-du-Loup. While there I met some people from the area. Shortly before the proposal was made by Petro-Canada to the NEB, this proposal was amended to include Canso in Nova Scotia, another possible site for the terminal. It is clear, Madam Speaker, that there is a conflict here between the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) concerning this site. I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson):
That the choice of the terminal site be referred to the Commons national resources committee in order to ascertain the pros and cons. I beg of both ministers to put an end to their chess game.

Madam Speaker, my question to the Prime Minister also relates to a question of constitutional responsibility which needs public airing.
Where there may be a conflict regarding the release of information before a royal commission in this country and the very clear duty and responsibility of a provincial attorney general to prosecute or, at the very least, to have an investigation where serious allegations of a criminal nature have been made, which in the view of the Prime Minister and the government takes paramountcy? Is it the right of a royal commission to decline to release information to a provincial attorney general, or is it the right and responsibility of a provincial attorney general to prosecute?

Madam Speaker, the question oversimplifies the problem. There are two sovereign governments involved and each has its own responsibility. Speaking for this government, a royal commission was established which has been asked to get to the bottom of the incidents involving the RCMP. The work of the commission is proceeding on course. It will report by next March 31, and as has been indicated many times in this House, the government will take its responsibility with that report.

Madam Speaker, I am curious as to why the Prime Minister, who claims to have a very serious knowledge of the law of this country and constitutional questions, would not answer that question.
My supplementary question to the Prime Minister relates, of course, to the long letter sent to the Minister of Justice by the attorney general of Ontario. Other attorneys general across this country are also seriously concerned about the absence of full and complete disclosure, contrary to an undertaking given by the Clark administration to those attorneys general, of
information relating to very serious allegations of a criminal nature which would be given to them before the release of that information to the public.
I come back to the Prime Minister. Which in his mind has paramountcy when he, his Solicitor General, his Minister of Justice and 1 know that, in relation to the Checkmate matter in any event, in November, 1980, there is very little in those files which relates to national security matters.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member wants to know why I did not answer the first question. The answer is obvious. It was because the Solicitor General had the answer, and it was a perfectly satisfactory answer. We are faced with the problem of two levels of government having different areas of jurisdiction.
I repeat his words. As far as we are concerned as a government, we established a royal commission. We always, both in this House and outside the House, took the position that we would not intervene in the work of that commission, that we would not prejudge issues until the commission had reported, that we would not prosecute witnesses until the evidence was completely in or until the commission itself said that it was prepared to release the evidence. I think that is a perfectly acceptable and justifiable procedure, all the more justifiable, as the House knows, when the Solicitor General a very few days ago tabled an order in council indicating that we wanted the royal commission to bring in its final report by the end of March of next year, five months from now.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the government House leader. Will the House leader confirm that the kind of detail the government has in mind simply refers, for example, to the method of covering the proceedings of the House-that everything that is said by a speaker in the House has to be included, that there be no editing; and, second, that cameras or radio microphones will not be focused on people who are not being formally recognized by the Chair. Is that the kind of detail the government has in mind?

Those are good suggestions, Madam Speaker, and might I point out to the leader of the NDP that last week, when the members of the committee opposed their proceedings being televised, cer-

tain concerns were expressed. Some dealt with what the hon. member has just mentioned; others pertained to the application of certain principles such as, respecting the electronic Hanzard, bilingualism and simultaneous translation.
Other matters will also have to be discussed, such as how the proceedings will be televised, the problems of setting up subcommittees. The hon. member will understand that for the sake of efficiency the committee might well decide to break up into various groups with a view to hearing the largest possible number of witnesses; the question might well come up then of which of those groups should have its proceedings televised. I feel it might be wise for the House leaders to try to avoid them and, ultimately, find an arbitrator who could make the decisions should problems arise.
In concluding, might I say that our favouring, at this time, the televising of the proceedings of the joint committee should in no way be interpreted as a means of delaying, in any way, the work or the report of the committee.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Order.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: The minister has stated in this House that the most severe difficulties are faced by those young people who cannot get their first entry into the job market and that he has to tackle that problem immediately. With unemployment in the 15 to 24-year-old age bracket now at 13.4 per cent, up dramatically since the minister decided to tackle the problem, and with 15,000 more unemployed in September-as a matter of fact, 2,000 fewer employed than a year ago-can the minister tell us how much longer the young people of Canada have to wait for action from this obviously uncaring government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to point out to the hon. member that since this time last year well over 230,000 jobs have been created in this country. That is a very important fact.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Furthermore, because of the number of cancellations and cutbacks the hon. member's government instituted, opportunities for young people, women and others to work in direct employment were cut back. We have had to put those programs back into effect, as we have now done, and they are now being implemented and providing a number of new work opportunities.
1 further point out to the hon. member that we have initiated a major task force chaired by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, and a number of assessments are going on in our department to provide the kinds of changes which we all recognize must take place in order to respond to new work conditions in the 1980s. So 1 think we are a caring government. We are concerned about unemployment but, unlike our predecessors, we are doing something about it.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister, who likes to put forward his programs as the panacea for all our problems but which provided only 12'A jobs in my riding where there are 5,000 on unemployment insurance. Hon. members opposite are really doing a great job!
The minister is hanging everything on this committee. Is he telling this House that he is not going to take any action at all until that committee reports but that he will take action on that committee's report and follow its recommendations?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, unlike the hon. member opposite, I would like to have the facts before I make decisions. 1 think it is important when we establish a committee of Parliament made up of members on both sides of the House that we pay them the proper respect and wait for them to bring forward their findings before going ahead and taking major action. That was the purpose of having the committee.
However, in the meantime we have started a number of programs this year which are providing employment opportunities. There are special programs for women in training, a special native training program, and the community development program which replaces the one cancelled by the hon. member's government.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Twelve jobs in my riding.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
The fact is that these programs are providing close to 50,000 jobs across this country, which is a very important step forward. We believe it is very essential at this time that we make a very careful assessment of the job market as it will appear in the years ahead and respond to it properly.
I also suggest to the hon. member that in the budget presented by the Minister of Finance two weeks ago an additional $350 million was allocated to deal with job problems and industrial problems in this country, and we intend to be making announcements on that very soon.

subsubtopic: ROLE OF CANADIAN-OWNED OIL COMPANIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. It relates to the position of Canadian-owned, independent oil companies under the new energy program of the government. One of the objectives of this program is to increase the degree of Canadian ownership of the oil and gas industry in Canada, which is an objective we on this side of the House fully support.

Oral Questions
Development was-and I am using his word-"distorted", 1 wonder if the minister could also tells us whether he feels that the council's documented view that increased unemployment also means an increase in marriage breakdown, crime, and suicide is also distorted.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-REPORTED VIEW OF CANADIAN COUNCIL ON SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: For young people?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-REPORTED VIEW OF CANADIAN COUNCIL ON SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: In fact, the increase has been about 2.2 per cent year to year. The unadjusted unemployment level is precisely the same this month as it was a year ago. These are a number of encouraging signs which I invite the hon. member to place against the concern we all feel about increased unemployed at whatever level.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-REPORTED VIEW OF CANADIAN COUNCIL ON SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I invite the minister to go to downtown ridings and to areas of high unemployment-there is over 25 per cent unemployment among young people in my riding-and give that kind of complacent statement to young people hanging around and looking for jobs.
My supplementary question is for the same minister. In light of the announcement made today by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that the community services program of CMHC will be cancelled entirely, and in light of the fact that the minister in his budget statement announced an increase in taxation by way of an increase in unemployment insurance contributions of $1 billion, thereby, in the words of his colleague, the hon. member for Lincoln, shifting the tax burden from one group of taxpayers to another, those least able to afford it, I should like to ask the minister what is the logic of this at a time when unemployment is increasing?

Indeed, as I understand it the language was much more colourful than that.
My question of privilege arises out of a question directed to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion by my hon. friend from Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). In responding not only did the minister evade the matter, but now through the press he has misled the Canadian people. subsubtopic: GROS-CACOUNA-ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext:
1.	Have any undertakings or commitments been made by the government or the National Harbours Board in respect of the development of Gros-Cacouna on the St. Lawrence River and, if so, what are they?
2.	Have any proposals been made by or to the government or the National Harbours Board whereby Gross-Cacouna will become a terminal or transshipment point for petroleum, gas or bulk products?
3.	What control does the government exercise, directly or through an agency, over the development of Gros-Cacouna and who owns the facilities now in place?

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: GROS-CACOUNA-ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext:
1. A general cargo terminal is under construction at Gros-Cacouna. The terminal will provide year-round shipping facilities to accommodate local and regional industries. Dredging of berth approach and turning basin is completed, as well as the construction of the wharf and storage area. A 25,000 square foot shed is being built and should be completed by December, 1980. Transport Canada will assume the administration of the facilities upon acceptance of the certificate of completion. The facilities are owned by the Federal Government and the Department of Public Works has responsibility for the realization of this project.
2. Following a proposal by Misener Holdings Limited to develop a dry bulk deep water terminal at Gros-Cacouna, Transport Canada, Misener Holdings Limited, Havre Champlain Incorporated and the provincial government entered into
an agreement and signed leases on January 31, 1980. Misener Holdings Limited and Havre Champlain Incorporated have proposed a three-phase development program for a dry bulk terminal. A conceptual plan must be completed and submitted to Transport Canada within 12 months of the execution of the agreement. For the purpose of the signature of a lease with the province of Quebec, Phase III has been divided and is now referred to as phase III and phase IV. Gros-Cacouna figures among ports of the maritime region and lower St. Lawrence River under consideration by Trans-Canada Pipeline and Petro-Canada for developing a liquefied national gas terminal. The project is still being studied by the companies.
3. The Government of Canada, under authority of the Canada Shipping Act and the Government Harbours and Piers Act has control over the development of Gros-Cacouna. Pursuant to order in council No. AC 644 of April 5, 1966, and No. 1852 of June 27, 1979, land and water lots have been transferred to Canada by Quebec and Quebec has authorized Canada to lease such land and water lots to Misener Holdings Limited and Havre Champlain Incorporated. Canada is also leasing to Misener Holdings Limited and Havre Champlain Incorporated, certain federal land and water lots for this development, and is committed to dredge the approach channel and turning basin to a depth of forty feet. The cost of the dredging, estimated at $6.9 million, will be recovered from the company over a period of years.

Unfortunately, credit unions, other financial institutions and trust companies are not given equal opportunity with the life insurance companies. This should be changed so that people have an opportunity to purchase more realistic programs. The credit unions and other Canadian financial institutions would be stronger if they were allowed to provide greater service and thereby compete more fully with the banks. Again we are back to the business of a cheque. Basically I am suggesting we should amend this legislation and put clear signals in it indicating that we want equality with respect to the credit unions, banks and other financial institutions so that we are not specifically biasing competition in favour of foreign banks. Mr. Speaker, not in any way for the reasons outlined by the proposal of this amendment, I wish to argue that a definition of the word "cheque" should be included at this point in the Bank Act.
I used the word "cheque" in my amendment in the definition of a bank. It seems to me that it follows logically the amendment of the hon. member which we are discussing now. The definition of the word "cheque" follows logically and in sequence within this bill. I find extraordinary the mental contortions of the draftsmen who have said that they will put in the definition of a bank. They have broadened the definition of a bank contained in the Bills of Exchange Act by saying that a bank within the meaning of the Canadian Payments Association Act will include a credit union. I invite the minister, who is not a lawyer, to say that part of good law and well-prepared law is that it shall appear clearly. If a person, other than a person who has been exhaustively briefed, were asked by a client for the legal definition of the word "cheque",

November 12, 1980
Bank Act
1 defy the minister to tell me that that person could turn to the Bills of Exchange Act to find a definition of it.
We are dealing with the Bank Act and its very exhaustive definitions clause, which is where I tried to put in the word "bank" and the business of banking. What does agricultural equipment mean? What about agricultural implements, beneficial interest, beneficial ownership, a bill of lading, a branch, a central co-operative credit society, a corporation, a court, crops, farms? Everything in connection with the Bank Act has a legal definition, except the business of banking which is its heart and core.
In my definition of a bank, 1 used the word "cheque". As the minister can readily understand, my definition, on which we will vote in due course, indicates that "bank" means any financial institution engaged in the business of lending money and accepting deposit liabilities transferable by cheque or other instrument. Any trained lawyer will say that is fine, but first of all he would like to know what are deposit liabilities and what is a cheque. The hon. member who spoke before me satisfied that lacuna by his definition of "cheque" in the definitions clause within the Bank Act. For that reason I support it, not for some of the reasons he suggested, but in the logical development of the Bank Act.
In committee I agreed with him that we should have a definition. I supported this idea in committee. But I find it strange that we must go to the Bills of Exchange Act in order to find some reference to what is a bank. It includes every member of the Canadian Payments Association established under the Canadian Payments Association act. What a horse's neck way of defining a bank! Anyone belonging to the Canadian Payments Association is a bank. It is not so.
That is the most convoluted thinking possible, and I will say without any equivocation that it is firmly fixed in my mind that as a result of the discussions and arguments I have had both in committee and in private with regard to this question of a definition of a bank within the Bank Act every effort has been used by government draftsmen to try to get around the logic and the necessity of responding to my arguments.
The actions of the government with regard to this just do not hold water. The government has some idea that somewhere, somehow, some court may some day establish a definition for a bank or what should be the business of banking. We get a half-hearted definition of a bank or a partial definition of a bank in clause 92, which appears at page 447 of Bill C-6, so a credit union is used or brought in to answer the very logical problem put forward by the proposer of this amendment. But it would have been much simpler to have accepted the amendment in its place in the definitions clause without having to go to this convoluted language of clause 92 when no one will really go and look to find whether any definition exists for what is a cheque and whether a cheque is an order for payment drawn on a credit union.
Now that the credit unions can appear within the Canadian payments association, certainly the document which is drawn
by a credit union member and which is a cheque, since it transfers funds from the account of the depositor to a third party, must be defined as a cheque, and therefore the logic in the requirement is quite right. But why do it this way? It is merely, I think, because to do it in the way which would be the shortest and the most logical would be to admit to the logic 1 have been putting forward to the government for these many long months with regard to the definition of a bank and the business of banking.
I am going to support this amendment. Of course, it follows through, because if the amendments which are the subject of my motions Nos. 1 and 2 hopefully carry, then No. 3 must carry. They are complementary, and they would make for a much more intelligent bill than the one before us at the present time. For that reason I wish to support the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, very briefly, I would like to go over some of the arguments that I have used before the standing committee to explain why the government is against the proposal made by the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) to include the definition of "cheque" in the list of definitions found in the first part of this bill to revise the Bank Act. First, the hon. member for Comox-Powell River used some arguments which, I agree with the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), are not really relevant to the definition or to the usefulness of including such a definition in that part of the legislation.
The hon. member for Edmonton West suggested that for the sake of logic, we should try to establish a sort of continuity at the beginning of the bill between the definitions of bank, banking activity and cheques. I should like to tell him that 1 am inclined to agree with him, but that in addition to logic, there is also a matter of method or rather of methodology involved here. But let us consider first the logic. The hon. member will doubtless recognize that the definition itself and the fact that it appears at the beginning of the bill bear witness to the fact that it belongs to the generality, that it is a generic term. One moves from the general to the particular, and the definition of cheque, as has been mentioned, appears in the Bills of Exchange Act, a legislation of wide application which therefore covers to a certain extent the definition in the Bank Act, and is limited by the Bank Act itself. In other words, as far as logic is concerned, the generality of the Bills of Exchange Act provides a general definition for the term "cheque" which applies in this case to the Bank Act, which governs certain types of institutions defined in the act.
It was said there would be a problem, from a methodological point of view, in including strict definitions of bank, banking activity, and consequently, cheque. We got around the methodological difficulty-and the hon. member for Edmonton West or the hon. member for Comox Powell might say it is a distortion, but it is a methodological detour-by borrowing
November 12, 1980

from a text of general application such as the Bills of Exchange Act, where there is a definition of "cheque" and the meaning of the term "bank" is extended to members of the Canadian payments association, and we know the local credit unions, such as the caisses populaires will be covered by this amendment to section 92 of the Bills of Exchange Act.
So to get around the problem regarding powers, another method or another act is used. The caisses populaires and credit unions, being members of the Canadian payments association will meet the requirements that will enable them to have a certain type of activity or wider activities, and the term "cheque" as it appears in the Bills of Exchange Act will apply to those institutions since they belong to the Canadian payments association, which is what the amendment is seeking.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that this only seems to be a problem because, as the hon. member is well aware, the Bank Act has a much more restrictive definition which includes only the institutions to which the act expressly applies, while from a methodological standpoint, to cover the opening made to caisses populaires and credit unions by the Canadian payments association, another definition is used for a very specific reason in another act.
I would like to refer to a few of the arguments made by the hon. member for Comox-Powell River which did not concern directly the matter of definition. For instance, 1 do not really see how a definition of the word "cheque", such as requested by the hon. member, would bring about more competition among chartered banks. I believe that, basically, this new legislation promotes competition because it makes it easier for financial institutions to become banks under the terms of the act. Second, it allows many financial institutions for instance, foreign financial institutions, to apply to become banks through letters patent. Third, this legislation creates the Canadian payments association which will enable the caisses populaires and credit unions to get fully involved in the types of activities which were previously restricted to the banks under the Canadian banking legislation or in activities in which chartered banks were more generally involved. I believe that it is basically these three elements which will promote more competition among banking institutions and within banking activities. And even though the definition proposed by the hon. member does not seem at first glance to create any problem within the legislation, it unfortunately does so.
Bank Act
For instance, the caisses populaires come under provincial jurisdiction. Even though they may, if they so request, become members of the Canadian payments association, they do not come directly under the federal legislation as financial institutions, and this is the type of problem that we want to avoid by implementing a different series of definitions for methodological purposes, and the hon. member will certainly understand that this takes nothing away from the competitiveness and the qualities of caisses populaires and credit unions.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) is suggesting, 1 think, by moving this amendment is quite simple. He is attempting to define a term which is used in the act without definition at present. I can remember in the committee when we were discussing this matter just prior to taking a vote, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) asking, "Why should we define a term in the Bank Act when that term is not in fact used in the act?" He thought he had come up with the best objection possible to adopting what I would have thought was a relatively simple and uncontroversial definition of "cheque". It was pointed out to him that the word "cheque" is, in fact, used in the Bank Act. It appears, for example, at pages 310 and 311 of Bill C-6, in clause 303, paragraphs (a) and (b). That is just one example and there are others. So what we find is the use of the word "cheque" in the act without a definition, which I would have thought was not something government draftsmen would greatly desire. The definition put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Powell River, is quite straightforward. It simply says that "cheque" means a bill of exchange drawn on a bank, a savings bank, a trust company or a credit union, payable on demand. The reason for putting that in is partly practical and partly symbolic. The practical implications are obvious when we consider that many government cheques and so on should not, in our view, specify that they are simply cashable at a chartered bank or at any of a number of financial institutions of which chartered banks are only one. Credit unions and caisses populaires are others. In our view it makes a great deal of sense, both practical and symbolic, to admit that we have a plural financial system, that we have a Bank Act which does not discriminate against trust companies and credit unions with respect to the use of the word "cheque" and the concept of a cheque and which encourages these financial institutions in their growth. As my hon. friend from Comox-Powell River has pointed out, we are anxious to see the credit unions and caisses populaires treated fairly and not in a discriminatory fashion by the government. So I cannot for the life of me see why we do not accept the definition.

Mr. Speaker, I too support the amendment before us. I think it is important for some of the reasons which have been outlined by the previous speakers and also because it would make it possible for the credit unions in this country to operate more competi-

tively. The objective of this bill when it was introduced in the House was to increase competition in the banking field. The apparent thrust of that move toward more competition seems to have been aimed at introducing foreign banks to the Canadian climate rather than increased use of the banking institutions and near banking institutions we have here. There is a great need for changes to the act so as to enable this kind of competition to be brought about. How serious is the government about introducing more competition? We look at the bill as it has come out of committee and we find there is no definition of the word "cheque" and no proper recognition of the fact that credit unions can provide a great many of the services which banks provide. Is the government really prepared to consider the institutions which have been developed in this country, namely, the credit unions and the caisses populates? Are their needs to be considered or is it the intention only to consider the needs of the foreign banks? What changes are the government proposing to make to the existing legislation? What changes are they talking about which would bring about equality in the competition?
The competitive disadvantages for credit unions are fairly well known, but I would like to list some of them. For instance, there are the legislative restrictions under the Financial Administration Act which prevent the deposit of federal government funds in financial institutions other than chartered banks. The Canadian Wheat Board Act permits elevator and grain companies, authorized by the board, to borrow from chartered banks but not from credit unions. The Livestock and Livestock Products Act requires livestock commission agents to keep a shippers trust account in a chartered bank but not in a credit union or caisse populaire. The Bills of Exchange Act defines a cheque as a bill of exchange drawn on a bank. This is the kind of thing we are talking about with respect to the Bank Act. We want to make certain that such cheques can be drawn on credit unions and trust companies as well.
There is also the Trust Companies Act, which I understand will be amended in the next six months or so. At the same time, the Cooperative Credit Associations Act, which is really complementary legislation, should also be opened up to allow for the broadening of the definition of the powers of a credit union. We believe one of the initial steps necessary to bring that about is to broaden the definition of "cheque" and the institutions which may handle such instruments under the new definition.
As we all know, credit unions have been clearing government cheques and orders at no cost. In some provinces this amounts to a fair sum of money. For instance, in my province of Saskatchewan credit unions provide 40 per cent of the clearings. In Quebec the caisses populaires cleared approximately 13 million items worth more than $2 billion in 1977. Yet credit unions and caisses populaires received no compensation for such work. It is true that the banks do not charge for clearing government orders but, at least, they have access to government deposits. This is something that all of the acts I have mentioned have in common-to specifically prevent the
deposit of government funds in credit unions. So the banks, at least, have the use of approximately $6.7 billion in deposits, which provide a considerable source of compensation in lieu of the services rendered. These are some of the reasons why we think we should begin by amending the Bank Act, to define a cheque and to include the credit unions and trust companies. We think it is an important beginning.
We also believe that further clean-up work should accompany this kind of change. We see it as an important beginning to reintroduce true competition in the made-in-Canada banking business. The credit unions and caisses populaires grew up in this country and we think that if we are to broaden and encourage competition in the banking business this is the one place we should start. We should broaden the definitions in the Bank Act so as to allow credit unions and caisses populaires to operate on the same basis as banks when it comes to clearing cheques.

Mr. Speaker, I will make a few comments on this particular definition. First of all, we on this side of the House have very little dispute with the hon. members' comments with respect to the credit unions and caisses populaires and their functions in the future financial system. The unfortunate thing is that much of what they have said is totally irrelevant to what we are talking about here, because this particular definition must be considered within the context of the act to which it relates. The act to which it relates is the Bank Act.
Unless hon. members opposite are willing to say that caisses populaires, credit unions, trust companies and savings banks, other than in the form of the Quebec Savings Banks, are in fact banks and therefore must be regulated under this act, then I would say that such a definition should in no way refer to institutions which are not related to the act to which the definition applies. The Bank Act relates only to banks and these other institutions are not a part of that and are not regulated by it.
The hon. member opposite said that a cheque should be defined and that credit unions, caisses populaires and trust companies should be allowed to issue cheques or have cheques drawn against their deposit liabilities. If that is the case then the proper place to do that is in a much more general statute which deals with the nature of bills of exchange. Lo and behold, on page 447 of the legislation before us this is precisely what the government proposes to do. It defines a cheque as a bill of exchange and includes, within that definition, bills of exchange drawn on and payable on demand from institutions other than banks. It does that in a direct way by simply saying for the purposes of the Bills of Exchange Act and for the purposes of this part of the Bills of Exchange Act a bank includes those institutions. That certainly does not mean that for the purposes of the Bank Act a bank includes those institutions. As a result, it is totally ludicrous to put a definition into the Bank Act which includes a reference to those very institutions that are not included as banks.
November 12, 1980

The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has indicated that this definition is consistent with his definition of a bank. I would suggest that it is not perfectly consistent with that definition because in that definition of a bank it says that a bank is an institution that draws or issues cheques or accepts cheques against their deposit liabilities. But below that particular portion his definition is that qualification that a bank does not include credit unions, caisses populaires, trust companies and companies covered by the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act. If they are not included, then why are we saying in the definition of a cheque, which comes in earlier, that in fact they are included? So the two are totally inconsistent.
I suggest that the government's approach of using the broader statute, which is the Bills of Exchange Act, as the vehicle for defining what a cheque is, so that institutions like credit unions, caisses populaires, trust companies and others can participate in this financial system using vehicles such as cheques, is the appropriate way of going about this. It certainly makes no sense to put a definition in the Bank Act which refers to institutions which are not banks and are not covered by the Bank Act. This being said, I would suggest that the amendment be defeated.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on this subject. I fear that the consequence of the amendment if accepted would be something the mover of the motion does not want. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friends have mentioned, this amendment deals not only with practicalities, but with symbols. It acknowledges a principle in which I and hundreds of thousands of people in this country have believed for a long time. It is not just a case of people working for money, but of money working for people. I would like to inform the hon. member opposite who has just spoken that 60 per cent of all cheque clearing in the province of Saskatchewan is done through the credit union movement and that the other 40 per cent is divided among trust companies, chartered banks, etc.
Dealing with credit unions comes from a tradition of long, bitter experience with banks, trust companies and finance companies. In fact, there should be a law against any finance company using the word "beneficial" because it is a total contradiction when one looks at the way in which they operate.
Bank Act
The credit unions of Saskatchewan were the first, ahead of the chartered banks, trust companies or other financial institutions, to institute computer automatic bank tellers. Since the credit unions clear 60 per cent of all the cheques, surely the definition of cheques as they are handled and printed by credit unions, should be included in the Bank Act.
I have here my cheque book. The contents are called cheques and they are printed by the Sherwood Credit Union Limited, Regina, Saskatchewan. I do not deal with banks. It seems to me that whether it is a case of my clearing a cheque or a case of half the population of Saskatchewan clearing its cheques through credit unions, they should damn well be recognized as such in the Bank Act. The story of why I now deal only with credit unions began when I was a young married man with a job and three kids, owing bills all over town and trying to raise my first loan. The banks and finance companies would not lend me a nickel unless I owned some property such as a house or a farm. They wanted to know my assets when all I had was my salary and my good name. A credit union came through and helped me out within a matter of 20 hours, and I have never been to a bank since, nor do I have any intention of ever going to a bank.
What we are talking about is money working for the people, not just people working for money. I hope the government will reconsider and accept this amendment because it will do no horrendous damage to its idea of what should be banking legislation for Canada. However, it will finally give full and proper recognition, which is long overdue, to the day-to-day practice of credit unions and what is occurring in Saskatchewan and Quebec, the provinces where most credit unions and caisses populaires are found.
In fact, I hope credit unions become so abundant that some of the chartered banks and other private financial institutions gradually disappear. What they do, and the way in which it is done, are irrelevant to the needs of people when it comes to money working for people. The introduction of automatic bank tellers means that the several thousands employees of the federal government in Saskatchewan can go down to their credit union lobby and deposit a government cheque after normal banking hours. Credit unions have made use of the latest technology and it is working marvellously well.
I. do not see any reason why, when there are areas such as Saskatchewan and Quebec in which the overwhelming majority of financial transactions by ordinary people occur with credit unions and caisses populaires, there should be no recognition given to credit unions in the Bank Act. What is the government worried about? If it wishes to amend some other legislation or include the matter in some other legislation, then that is fine.
Credit unions are people's banks. We call them credit unions because we think it is a much better term. Credit unions evolved because hundreds of thousands of Canadians across this country had bitter experiences with banks in the strictest sense of the word. They were formed by the people. Credit unions did not come out of Bay Street in Toronto or James Street in Montreal; they came out of the people.

November 12, 1980
Bank Act
Credit unions print their own cheques. They are cheques in fact, if not in law, so why do we not provide some kind of recognition by putting in place a symbol of what is a fact in this country? People from all walks of life, small businessmen, farmers, workers, old age pensioners and so on, bank at credit unions. I invite hon. members, particularly those on the government side who have dealings with the Bank Act, to visit the approximately ten branches of credit unions which thrive in the little city of Regina. They will see what credit unions mean to the people of that city and how these institutions operate.
The amendment proposed by my colleague, does nothing more than to bring up to date what is practice and tradition for several millions of Canadians from coast to coast. It is a practice which is growing in every province and region of this country. I do not understand the reluctance of the government to recognize this reality, face up to it and include my colleague's amendment in the Bank Act. Surely, the experience of the credit union movement, which 1 am sure has been brought to the attention of many hon. members opposite, with regard to the clearing of cheques by central banks, the kicks in the teeth it received from the banking association over the years and the attempts of the banks to discriminate, inhibit or make more awkward the operations of credit unions and caisses populaires to deal fully and completely with every aspect of a member's financial dealings, must be recognized in an updated Bank Act.
1 do not understand the obfuscation put up by the hon. gentleman across the way a few moments ago. 1 do not understand why he has not recognized that the Bank Act, the primary financial legislation of this country as it pertains to financial institutions, should cover the point made by my hon. friend who moved the amendment. When I use the word "symbolic", 1 do not mean it lightly. It is a very important and serious symbol to many people in this country. Even if in most instances it is a minor detail and means little or nothing in day to day practice, the fact that it is there means a great deal to a lot of people.
I hope the government will reconsider and that the minister and his colleagues will say, "What the heck, there is no harm in having this." There is no harm to whoever it is they are trying to help. There is a benefit to the credit union and the caisses populaires employees of this country contained in this amendment. We do not move the amendment lightly nor without a great deal of consultation with our friends in the credit unions and the caisse populaire movement. We would not, and we do not, move it just on our own. This is not just socialist dogma, Mr. Speaker. It comes from people across party lines-in my province anyway-who say they want this sort of thing in the Bank Act. I hope the minister will reconsider and say it is all right, that he does not think it does harm to the government's bill. They may still wish to disagree but it may not mean that much to the credit unions and caisses populaires in Canada. He might be right in that; I do not know, but surely we could agree it will not do any damage to
the legislation. Its passage may or may not be helpful to the credit union movement in this country.
On those grounds alone, Mr. Speaker, if for none of the other reasons that I have illustrated, I hope the government will accept this amendment.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this amendment is quite simple. We take a different view from that of the government with respect to the process of incorporation. One of the things this act does is to allow a process of incorporation to take place without requiring parliament itself to authorize a particular charter. I say to the minister that we would be prepared to withdraw this motion if he would be prepared to reconsider his position on motion No. 6. In other words, we made some progress in committee when we accepted the amendment from the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) dealing with the question of the right of the Inspector General of Banks to hold an inquiry concerning the incorporation process.
The minister will recall that the hon. member for Edmonton West was concerned, and we supported him, that if we are going to move from a process of parliamentary charter to a process whereby incorporation of a chartered bank would become very much like the incorporation of any other public company, there should be at least some kind of hearing process. I have said to the minister on a number of occasions that if this legislation is passed as is, it will be easier to establish a chartered bank in Canada than to obtain a liquor permit in the province of Ontario.
The process by which one incorporates under the amendments put forward by the government does not require that the inspector general hold a hearing when he receives an objection,
November 12, 1980

but it gives the bureaucracy the right to decide whether the objections are of any importance and gives the inspector general the sole right, without having to hold a hearing, to determine whether the bona fides of those wishing to obtain a charter have been established.
In light of this, we would prefer a process whereby Parliament has a greater degree of control over the chartering of banks. We would prefer a continuation of the system whereby Parliament itself charters banks and each individual bank is subject to the strict scrutiny of Parliament and a parliamentary committee.
If this is not acceptable to the government, we are prepared to withdraw that motion and put forward the other motion. That is, if the government is not prepared to accept that principle, then at least require the inspector general-not to hold a hearing with regard to objections that have been made on the chartering of a bank-but to hold a public inquiry. Motion No. 6 in the name of the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) specifies that the inquiry shall be held in public, that upon completion of the inquiry the inspector general shall report his findings to the minister and that the minister shall make such report available to the public within 30 days.
In granting a charter to those who are determined to create a bank, one is, in fact, granting an extensive licence-a licence which in my view has far more impact on the public than a liquor license permit or a television station licence or any of a number of other activities. Yet the government tells us that there is no requirement to hold a public hearing at which objections can be heard in the case of chartering our banks.
This is not astonishing, because I know the faith the Liberal party has in the bureaucracy, and I know the lack of faith the Liberal party has in the concept of due process yet it is surprising to me, having regard to the advances in administrative law we have seen over the last 15 years in Canada, during which the courts have said, for example, that there is a duty of fairness, a duty to hold a hearing by all sorts of institutions when previously there was no such requirement. For example, it is no longer possible for a police officer to be deprived of his job without the right to a hearing; hospital boards, liquor licence tribunals, rent review tribunals, workmen's compensation boards, expropriation boards or any administrative institution established under the jurisdiction of the provinces or the federal government are subject to a requirement to be fair. There is a requirement to protect the public interest. There is a requirement to allow objections to be made. Authorities planning to build a public highway in the province of Ontario go before the municipal board. Every city that is involved in putting forward an official plan knows that people can make objections to it.
Mr. Speaker, I have more right with respect to the process of objections and the requirement of a public hearing to stop my neighbour from parking his car on his lawn than I have as a citizen of this country or a financial critic of this party, to question the bona fides of those who propose to establish a chartered bank. Yet the implications of the one decision are
Bank Act
much more vast and carry a far greater impact on the public than the question whether my neighbour can park on his lawn. It is amazing that the government can carry on in this way, just by a process of convincing themselves that there is no need to worry and that the bureaucracy can take care of everything. On other occasions the parliamentary secretary has said, "We do not want any yahoo coming in and objecting so that we will have to hold an inquiry." That is the typical Liberal attitude to objections from the public-that the public is necessarily illiterate; that the objections necessarily come from people who do not know what they are talking about and that the Government of Canada and the Liberal Party of Canada do not need to hear from those who object.
The Liberal party's attitude reminds me of the church before Vatican II. That is about the stage of their development. There is clearly a need for a Vatican II on that side of the House. There is clearly a need to let some light in, to let a little air in by having a public inquiry and not just, as the hon. member for Edmonton West has said, if the inspector general decides it might be worth while to give responsible citizens of Canada the chance to find out who the people are who want to establish a chartered bank, what their bona fides are, in which areas they plan to specialize, where they expect to gather their business and where they intend to invest in the future of Canada.
These are legitimate questions for Canadians to ask, Mr. Speaker. If we are not allowed to ask them in Parliament any more-and apparently such will be the case as a result of this act-then I think we should at least require the inspector general to hold a hearing and see that justice is done when a licence is granted to people to conduct a banking business, just as justice is required when licence is given to carry on all sorts of activities which give a substantial and substantive right to groups of individuals to engage in business in Canada.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question of the inquiry started out as a result of representations I had made. My views were coloured, first of all, by recognizing early on that there should be an alternative procedure to the road to Calvary which incorporators of banks were made to travel under the previous procedure of a private bill. I defy anyone to devise such a tortuous, expensive and frankly unnecessary system as the incorporation by private bill. All it took was two or three members, who were ideologically opposed to banks, to totally hamstring a legitimate operation and over the years, I saw that happen. The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) has never been aware of the thousands upon thousands of unnecessary expenses which were piled upon incorporators of banks in the past due to frivolous, and I would say, purely ideologically and devilishy inspired interference in the normal parliamentary process.
It was scandalous the way the parliamentary process was abused on certain occasions. Therefore, that method had to be eliminated. Now comes this proposal that a bank may be

November 12, 1980
Bank Act
incorporated, with all the other requirements, merely by letters patent. I insist also there should be some form of parliamentary control, if necessary. I have had experience of one or two incorporations, but if more light had been cast upon them in the early stages, as there was subsequently through probing questioning by members of the finance committee, the incorporations would have proceeded much more smoothly and regularly.
The amendment which appears as No. 6 in the name of the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood imposes a statutory obligation upon the Inspector General in the event of any objection-he does not say any valid objection. The world's greatest kook, or the most irresponsible, could object-and we know we have them. Anyone acting on a whim or for competitive purposes who wished to stall the application would merely have to file an objection with the inspector general who would then be bound to put the process of a public inquiry under way.
On the other hand, there could be valid objections. If members of the party of the sponsor of this amendment feel that any representations they might make, for example, against the incorporation of any particular bank, were not to be treated as valid or serious, and could be passed over casually by the Inspector General of Banks, then they place themselves perhaps in the right place at the right status. However, if they are going to be serious-and I am not necessarily saying they are not-and have a valid objection, on the basis of information, on the grounds that certain incorporators of a proposed bank were not persons of the quality required, or that there was some doubt about the source of funds, or for any number of valid reasons, they would have to come up with the proof. Mind you, they would have to realize that in making such allegation they would have to put their money where their mouth is. But that happens to anyone.
Let us look at the procedure to be followed by the inspector general and the minister under those circumstances. It must be remembered that under the letters patent procedure the application is filed and there are certain statutory requirements as to capital, the number of persons, the quality of those persons, and so on. The inspector general, of course, has sources by which he can make investigations about the character and backgrounds of the persons concerned. Let us assume that the applicants meet all those requirements. The Inspector General then has to make a recommendation to the minister, after which the further steps of incorporation can take place if all conditions are met. But if there were either verbal or written objections which appeared valid, there is not the slightest doubt in my mind that the Inspector General and the minister would insist upon a public inquiry. Take the possible case of either the Inspector General of Banks or the minister failing to recognize the validity or the seriousness of an objection and just issuing the permit. Subsequently the fact that there were valid objections to the permit to commence business would surface. Both individuals concerned would, I think, find themselves fired for dereliction of duty.
I know very well that the minister responsible for financial institutions would under no circumstances, if there were the slightest doubt, fail to hold a public inquiry. Therefore, I feel that by granting this discretion to a responsible official, by, in fact, imposing a duty on the minister in question to really have a hard look at the circumstances, we are protecting the public. Incidentally, we are also possibly protecting the incorporators who could find themselves facing malicious charges or malicious information. We cannot understand the motives of men at all times. Let us assume in this case that an application is made and there comes into the hands of the Inspector General or of the minister in question a letter or letters making certain allegations of a spurious nature. Pray, how could the minister, the Inspector General or the individuals involved disprove these spurious allegations? They may be smears or allegations as to past criminal records or bankruptcies. Not one of those individuals would have a venue to correct the record.
The Inspector General cannot do those things which he is not authorized to do. Neither can the minister. How would the record be cleared except by way of a public inquiry with the persons who make the allegations put on the stand to prove what they had said. To that extent I think there should be a public inquiry of the nature I proposed. I am told that concurrently a similar proposal was made in the Senate. I had no contact with it. I am glad the government saw the value of the proposal on the basis of the arguments advanced, not only to protect the public in the appropriate case, but to protect the minister and the Inspector General of Banks as well as those who would make a proposal under the act to incorporate a bank.
Therefore, the amendment incorporated in the bills reported is far superior to the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae). I understand his motives, but I respectfully differ from him in that his amendment would lay the operation of the act open to a great deal of mischief.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems we have slipped from motion No. 5 to No. 6 in the course of general consideration of a couple of amendments which would apply to the kind of principle we are attempting to get at. The first is basically the proposal which would remove from Parliament the right to consider the incorporation of a bank. My hon. friend outlined fairly clearly some of the dilemmas there.
It concerned us in committee that this is yet another removal from Parliament of a power exercised over very strong influences in our society. It is acknowledged that banks are very powerful players in the economy of Canada. What they do will shape all our lives. We are not dealing merely with a parking fine or the implementation of a by-law respecting the running of fences in a municipality where people are accorded the benefit of a public hearing. We are dealing with the removal of yet another right from Parliament to consider and provide input on very powerful players in our economy.
November 12, 1980

I have heard members on both sides stand up and say that this is of no consequence. In fact, when the government presented its original proposal, it wanted the inspector general to look at the circumstances, make recommendations to the minister and that was all. Parliament was no longer to have the responsibility. This was to be the procedure, they said. Very quick, very neat. On behalf of those who are trying to glean information from the government and ministers opposite,
I say, shame. Members across the way know the kind of record which has been established over the last year and, indeed, since the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came to power, yet they allow the erosion of yet another power of Parliament.
I am a new member of this institution. Since roughly 1968-69, the power to effectively control the estimates of the government has disappeared to a committee. The committees themselves have been hamstrung. Millions are spent on issues and items that cannot be properly examined because of a deliberately structured device to remove from Parliament the opportunity to consider them. Here is another example of erosion. It is being resisted by members who for more than ten years have fought against the government, the Prime Minister and some ministers about the erosion of the rights of Parliament.
The Inspector General of Banks is not responsible to the Canadian people for what goes on in the banks. It is the minister and the elected representatives here. We are responsible. We were sent to this Parliament to consider such matters. However, I see members of the official opposition allowing yet another erosion of the power of Parliament. This is of serious concern.
I mentioned our concerns about the Prime Minister. They deserve stating again. He has not played fair ball with the people of Canada in some of his actions. I call to the attention of hon. members the changes in our rules which had to be bashed home with closure. When they changed the rules, they removed the estimates and allowed Parliament to be hamstrung. I also recall the War Measures Act. In retrospect, the leader of that party stood up after it was over and stated he regretted the fact he had supported it at the time. That was a product of actions by that government, that Prime Minister and those ministers.
There is also the issue of the anti-inflation legislation. They made a commitment to the people that they would not introduce it, but once in power they jammed it through. That attitude is also reflected in the proposal before us. It is the erosion of another power of Parliament, and I am seriously concerned about it. The other day we sat through the closure motion. The government is not opposed to using closure, removing the powers of Parliament. We were seriously concerned about that. I congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for individually overcoming a very serious dilemma. The government in fact accepted it. It now lacks a single thing. Although it is a lesser solution, our amendments overcome it. The power is still largely removed from Parliament.
Bank Act
On the other side of the coin, the Inspector General has the discretion not to hold a public hearing "because there are kooks out there". What disturbs me is that over the years the government has said that the kooks are those who disagree with it. We all know where dissent is in a democracy. It is a very healthy procedure. It will not tie up or hamstring the business of this country to have people with serious concerns write those concerns down, submit them and have them considered at a public hearing.
Kooks are not going to be supported by large numbers of the public. People have the right to bring forward serious concerns about these powerful institutions. A major concern is that this procedure is not open enough. Second, there is an attitude which has been prevalent with this government-I do not think anyone here can deny it. They hold information very closely. They somehow feel it is not the right of Parliament and Canadians to have information. When it comes out, they feel it is politically damaging, and that is worse than providing the information. This provision still allows the basic offensive nature of the previous proposal put in by the government. Perhaps that is why it is there in only half its form, because it still gives the Inspector General of Banks the authority to do this. He can give notice to the minister involved, and the minister can say, "Do not do it". If we follow the legislation, we will realize that it has been removed now from the control of Parliament. Essentially we are faced with a continuing erosion of the powers of Parliament. Also we see a controlling of the entire process of incorporating banks by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) who undoubtedly will direct the Inspector General of Banks. We are very concerned about this particular item.
Allowing the amendment we have proposed to go through will broaden the very constructive amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) so that the government cannot compel the Inspector General to put it aside and say, "No, we do not want to expose it to the public". It compels the Inspector General, upon receipt of an objection, to hold a public meeting and allow concerned individuals to express their concerns in front of the press and in front of the people. Although the matter has been removed from Parliament, it is still compelled to remain within a public forum. No one in the House would disagree that banks are among the most prominent players in the economy. Foreign banks are among the most powerful institutions in the world, especially considering the leverage they will have over us.
This incorporation procedure is one of the most important issues of this act. Acceptance of our proposal will not harm anyone. The only objection was the one raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West, that perhaps a kook will submit an objection and therefore we should put a provision in the legislation giving absolute discretionary power to a public servant who in fact is manipulated-a poor choice of words- or guided by the Minister of Finance. Perhaps I will reselect that word.

November 12, 1980
Bank Act
If the House is prepared to accept our amendment, certainly no harm would follow. We will not see the banks hamstrung. They will not come streaming forward in droves trying to incorporate. We will not see the whole procedure hung up. In fact, there will be very few incorporations over a period of time. People will approach this new procedure very cautiously.

speechtext:
It only takes one to go down. I think we will see a very slow and easy incorporation procedure. If our amendment was adopted, these organizations would be required to go in front of the public when there was an objection. Certainly they cannot come before Parliament any more, but they could be made the subject of public scrutiny. There is no harm in that, despite the fears of the hon. member for Edmonton West.
I urge members of the House to accept this amendment. They are prepared on any municipal project to allow municipalities to hold public hearings, to allow the citizens to participate or at least to be informed about the decision-making and to register their objections so that concerned elected officials will know about them. This is not inconsistent with the legislation. The government is prepared to do it on sensitive environmental questions. I believe that on sensitive and serious economic questions affecting the way the economy will develop, who will control it and what are their objectives, we should allow the procedure to become public and not allow the government at will to suppress knowledge.
I urge members of the House to support this one small amendment which would allow the entire incorporation procedure to become a public process. If it does not happen, we shall not only be allowing the government to remove one further power from Parliament, as it has so many others, making this institution less effective in expressing the wishes of the people, but we shall also be depriving the public of the opportunity of having these powerful economic players appear before it on items of serious objection.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be brief. I have listened to the debate, to the points made both by my hon. friends and by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). I was struck by the unusual position put forward by the hon. member for Edmonton West. We are suggesting the provision of even a greater amount of protection for the public.
In order to understand the nature of our proposal, one must appreciate that members of the public have infinite confidence in the banking system. When they put their money in the bank, whether by way of purchasing shares or by deposit, they are confident in the belief that the banks operate under federal law which is written in such a manner that it is virtually impossible for the bank not to operate in a fiscally responsible way. When the hon. member for Edmonton West made his comments, I was struck by the confidence which he placed in the public service. He said that there may be some frivolous intervention. I draw the conclusion that because there may be some frivolous intervention, the public will get less protection
than it might otherwise be entitled to. The hon. member mentioned that it might be more costly to do it the way we are suggesting; because there may be an additional cost, the public are to have less protection than it might otherwise be entitled to. Because the member has confidence in the public service of today, he is saying in essence that the public of the future will have less protection than it might otherwise expect and heretofore has been entitled to.
Turning from banks for a few moments, I should like to look at the problems within financial institutions in general. Look at what happened in the most recent Astra Trust case-I want to point something out by way of example. I see the minister shaking his head. I am not suggesting a parallel can be drawn, but I am suggesting we ought to be encouraging a far greater degree of public scrutiny within all financial institutions, rather than lessening the degree of public scrutiny. I see the minister is now shaking his head affirmatively. He can understand why I draw that comparison, he can understand what I am driving at. In the case of trust companies, at the moment they are subject to approval, albeit provincial. There is a certain amount of federal involvement, but primarily it is provincial. People who had put their life savings into something they believed was protected by law discovered the protection was not worth the paper upon which it was written. There was no public hearing process in advance of that trust company being given the authority to conduct business and no mandatory process for advertising and public participation about which we are talking. If we take that extreme case today and extrapolate it over the next ten or 15 years, we would almost assuredly come up with the thought that a similar kind of thing could well occur within the banking structure.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: The Bank of Western Canada.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
My colleague mentions the Bank of Western Canada. A similar kind of thing could well occur within the banking structure under the system which is currently being proposed by the government and supported by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert).
What we are talking about is a guarantee that there will be the opportunity for public participation in perhaps the single most important area of the economy a guarantee that the sort of thing which happened to Astra, Reymor and the people who put their money there could not happen within the banking system. We are suggesting that if we adopted these simple amendments to ensure a public hearing, there would be scrutiny and an opportunity for the public, and those who might have knowledge, to take part in the process, thereby taking a step toward guaranteeing that this kind of failure and consequent hardship could never occur.
I ask the minister not to be impressed by the suggestion of the hon. member for Edmonton West that, because on an odd accasion there might be someone with frivolous intent who would attempt to subvert the process we would put other people in jeopardy over the course of years ahead, or that just because it might cost those who are asking for incorporation a
November 12, 1980

little more in terms of the dollars they would have to invest in order to go through the public hearing process we should run a risk unnecessarily. It was suggested that people might invest on the assumption that the government's guarantee stands behind a financial institution and that somehow or other, because it may cost a little more to go through that process, members of the public should have less protection in the future than that to which they are presently entitled, or, for that matter, because today's public service is working well and can be trusted with the responsibility this necessarily will always be the case in every instance.
We must write the law to protect the public, not the incorporators from a frivolous intervention, a costly hearing or from a civil service from which they need no protection. We must protect the public from situations which, at this point, we think might not occur but which, however, could well occur under the current legislation. That is what we are asking for, and it is simple. We are not talking about hearings every day of the week for the rest of our lives. We are not talking about incorporations being requested and applied for by the hundreds. We all know that this will not happen. We are talking about a reasonable number of hearings which will be held because we are committed to making sure that not just the banking structure but all of the financial institutions have to submit to the most rigorous set of requirements and present themselves before the public in order to justify the contention that they should be permitted to operate within the financial structure of Canada. That is what we are suggesting, and we are saying that this kind of amendment means further protection.
It is not just further protection; it is necessary protection. I am not suggesting for one moment that my comments are any more meaningful than those of anyone else, but in the light of these observations can the minister not see that we are courting potential danger in the future, that we are leaving a door open for failure in the banking system which we need not leave open? Rather than opening that door we should be closing other doors in an effort to protect the people of Canada who for some reason have great trust in the political system and believe that "guaranteed by the Government of Canada" means something. That is how they feel about banks. Incidentally, that is also how they felt about trust companies until fairly recently. For some reason they thought that because they were incorporated and given licences to operate by the government, the government would be looking into them with such care that there could be no way they could be ripped off by unscrupulous dealers. Unfortunately, the minister knows that has not been the case. I would have thought we would be moving to a more carefully thought out and more restrictive method of reviewing entry to the financial system of Canada rather than opening it up and leaving things to chance.
I therefore ask the minister in good conscience if he will not consider the representations made by both of my hon. friends and say, "Yes, you are right, there is, in fact, the chance that we may slip up, so let us close the loophole".

Mr. Speaker, we are discussing motions 4 and 6. I will first speak on motion No. 4 presented by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae). The effect of this motion would be to block one of the two avenues now open to an institution aiming at becoming a bank in the present sense of the law, since clause 7(a) states that an institution that wants to become a bank can still proceed through incorporation by Parliament as we do now and another option is added which is to proceed through letters patent. Motion No. 4 suggested by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood would do away with this second possibility, namely, to proceed through letters patent.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) say that the bill proposes to remove completely, from the process whereby a financial institution obtains the status of a bank, the right for Parliament to examine that incorporation. In fact, we are adding one more possibility, while keeping, as I pointed out before in subclause 7(2), the possibility of incorporation by both Houses. If that procedure is chosen by an institution, it is well understood that the public parliamentary examination now in current usage would apply.
However, another means is being put at the disposal of those institutions desirous of obtaining bank status and of falling under the jurisdiction of the federal Bank Act, and that is letters patent. For the first time, the Bank Act provides truly wide possibilities, which this really is, in the procedure allowing a financial institution to accede to bank status.
Much has been made in the course of our debate of certain public examinations. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) made much of the procedure those institutions will have to follow.
Mr. Speaker, hon. members are aware-or they will learn when they read clauses 12 and others following on page 18 of our bill-that before an application is made under subclause 7(1 )(b), a notice of intention to apply for the proposed letters patent and to operate as a banking institution under the Bank Act shall be published by the applicants for a period of four consecutive weeks in The Canada Gazette and in a newspaper published at the place where the head office of the bank is to be situated.
