Any person, as mentioned by the hon. member for Edmonton West, who has objections to the granting of letters patent to the people who have thus applied for them may write to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) or the Inspector General of Banks to advise them of his or her concern and request a public inquiry.
If we consider the procedure which appears in the text the committee submitted to the House, namely the amendment to clause 12, on page 18, which was largely based on the proposal made by the hon. member for Edmonton West, we note that

the only difference between the wording of subclauses (2), (3) and (4) and motion No. 6 proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Powell River appears in this part of the motion, and I quote:

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak on motion No. 5. That motion deals with the section of the act which specifies to whom letters patent incorporating a bank can be issued. Clause 8 reads as follows:
Notwithstanding subsection 7(2), letters patent incorporating a bank shall not be issued
(a) to Her Majesty in right of Canada or in right of a province, to any agent or employee of Her Majesty in either such right, or to any corporation owned or controlled by Her Majesty in either such right;
I find it ironic that the government would be taking such an ideological position with respect to the next ten years in our banking legislation. I do not see why the government should rule out of court the question as to whether or not a province should be allowed to incorporate a chartered bank-and I will come to the reasons why that may be a very good idea-or why the government should not be allowed to establish a Crown bank if it were found to be one way of increasing competition in the absence of competition coming from other sectors, or if it is found to be one way in which the government can reorganize its granting of concessionary or other special kinds of loans to a number of special interest groups, such as farmers, small businessmen, people involved in housing or others.
I want to deal with each of those two points. The first is with respect to the ability of the provinces to engage directly in the business of banking by incorporating a federally chartered bank. It is one of the realities in our country that our largest chartered banks, the "Big Five" as they are called, which have such a stranglehold on the banking business and indeed on
Bank Act
many aspects and many parts of capital markets today, are regarded by many Canadians as the representatives of a particular part of Canada, as simply being institutions for the benefit of central Canada which, in a historic sense, have sucked up savings from Canadians right across the country and largely to the profit of those who live in central Canada. Indeed, I think it is one of the perceptions of our country which has a detrimental effect not only on our financial life but also on our political and social life. As a result of the boom in oil and natural gas in western Canada it is no longer the case that the west is without economic resources. Indeed, it is the fastest growing part of the country, economically, and the economic power of the west which is growing very rapidly. It is growing so rapidly that the province of Alberta has developed a heritage fund worth somewhere in the area of $8 billion at the present time. The value of the fund grows daily and it will be further increased by the additions to the price of oil and gas which have just been tabled in the House of Commons by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde).
One of the key questions is that of the fiscal imbalances which these revenues create in our economic system, the fiscal relationship between the federal and provincial governments. It is one of the intractible problems of the decade and one of the great challenges of the 1980s. It has become unrealistic to say to the government of Alberta, or to the people of Alberta: you can create your credit unions and your provincial savings offices, which function in a sense as savings banks for individual Albertans, but you're not allowed to become directly involved in the business of chartering a bank. I find it hard to understand how a party which prides itself on being pragmatic and responsive to events and on being one which does not take any ideological position, would say that under no circumstances will provincial governments be allowed to incorporate federally-chartered banks. The ironic consequence of taking this ideological position will be that the federal government will have less control over capital markets than would be the case were they to allow the provincial governments to become directly involved in the federally-controlled and legislated business of banking. I am thinking particularly of the provincial government of Alberta, but it could be the provincial governments of Saskatchewan or British Columbia. I find it ironic that the federal government, a Liberal government, is requiring that the governments of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia-indeed, any provincial government-establish not federally-chartered institutions but provincial institutions. For example, six or seven years ago, when Mr. Barrett's government wanted to establish a financial institution which would reflect the needs and demands of the economy of British Columbia and which would be able to deal directly with the problems of small businesses and consumers-problems which were not being dealt with by the chartered banks-he was not able to establish a federally-chartered bank. Instead, he was required to establish a provincially-incorporated trust company. I find it ironic that because it is taking an ideological position with respect to the formation of Crown banks, wheth-

November 12, 1980
Bank Act
er they be provincial or federal, a Liberal government should be guaranteeing that the recycling process take place, which is so critical, is going to take place entirely outside federal jurisdiction. It is a phenomenon which is, indeed, passing strange.
It is also a strange phenomenon that the federal government would be tying its hands in this way by saying that under no circumstances will we consider in the next ten years the possibility of forming a federally-chartered Crown bank. I say this because ministers opposite has often said they pride themselves on their lack of ideology with respect to the formation of Crown institutions. In fact, they have nationalized whole areas of economic life. The Conservative party did precisely the same thing. It makes me smile to hear Conservative friends on my right mounting opposition to any direct federal or government involvement in the economy when it was a Conservative government which created such institutions as the Bank of Canada and the CBC.
It was the Liberal government which authorized the takeover of de Havilland and which created many Crown corporations from Polysar to Polymer and countless others. Now they are telling us that this kind of Liberalism is dead and is being replaced by a more hard line kind of Conservatism which means they are not going to become involved in the economy in this way any longer. They say this in spite of the variety of consumer services provided by our chartered banks, whether in fact the chartered banks are providing the services they could provide to small business, farmers, or consumers right across Canada or whether they are providing the services they could to fishermen in Atlantic Canada or to northern communities which are essentially isolated and without financial institutions. The federal government is saying that under no circumstances will it ever consider the possibility of creating a federally-chartered institution, at least for the life of the Bank Act. Frankly, I do not see the logic of the government's position, other than to suggest that it is a purely ideological one. Ministers over there are not prepared even to consider the possibility of allowing provinces to get involved in their banking institutions and to play as great and as active a part in the financial life of the nation as central Canadians have played for the last hundred years. I find it passing strange that they would be tying their own hands at a time when a great many Canadians are asking questions with respect to the services being provided to them by the largest chartered banks.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say something at this point because all the other amendments I have go further than the strictures in the act. The act does not allow a federal or provincial government to incorporate a bank under a letters patent process. That is the section which is being amended. The objective of the amendment is to delete that prohibitive clause. On the other hand, in the act there are already provisions which allow a government to participate-up to 25 per cent-in the incorporation of a bank. That is a grandfather proposition. It was a pay-off.
There was the WEOC Conference in Calgary some years ago. It pre-dated the Hon. John Turner leaving the government, so it would be about 1973. To please Mr. David Lewis and the NDP, as well as Mr. David Barrett, the Premier of British Columbia, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated that the Bank Act would ultimately be amended to allow for the incorporation and establishment of a chartered bank in British Columbia. Subsequently, but without the knowledge of Mr. Turner, the Prime Minister broadened this to actually purchasing an interest in an existing chartered bank.

speechtext: You could speak-

speechtext:
If a government member wishes to take part in the debate, he should also rise. He can understand me, we are in a bilingual country and since most people in my area are English-speaking it is natural for me to speak to them in English. However, if the member wants me to do so I will take up the time of the House and repeat everything I say. In that specific case, since I am dealing with a rather Anglophone issue, I will speak in English.
In an attempt to please British Columbia, the intent was to allow that province to buy into an existing bank, much to the horror of the then minister of finance. When the Bank Act came down with a white paper, fortunately reason had prevailed and the reference to purchasing an interest in an existing bank had disappeared. It was due mostly to the fact that by that time the heritage and trust fund had begun. It was obvious that if the province of Alberta were so minded, it could likely go out and buy the control of any chartered bank in the country. Economically, for all the reasons in the world-and I do not have to repeat those reasons which I put on the record at the time of the incorporation of the Bank of British Columbia and subsequently-I am unalterably opposed to the Government of Canada or to the government of any province having any interest in a charter bank.
According to this legislation, governments are allowed to become involved in new banks, not the existing banks, up to 25 per cent after a period of time. Governments would even be in better shape than any other corporate shareholders whose maximum involvement can only be to the extent of 10 per cent. There is a conflict of interest. With a holding of that size, a government as a shareholder would be entitled to one or more directors on the board. At that point, the government would have direct access to the business affairs of all the clients of that bank. Suppose the bank had interests beyond provincial boundaries and proposals were put forward by a particular client for financing an expansion either in one province or another. It would come to the attention of the government-appointed directors that a business proposed to borrow money from the bank to assist it in establishing a business in other than the province which had a share in that bank, at which point the squeeze can be put into effect-the government could insist that the development take place in that particular
November 12, 1980

province, all other things being equal other than, shall we say, the location of a particular resource or raw material.
Each of the provinces has a department of industry, trade and commerce, and it is up to those departments to illustrate the advantages to industry of locating in the particular province. It is up to that government through such a department or departments to put legislation on the books which will offer to the public generally incentives to establish a business in that particular province. Certainly, it should not at any time be within the powers of any government to use the leverage which it will have on the board of directors of a bank to direct investment into or out of a particular province under a "beggar thy neighbour" policy.
I cannot for the life of me see how that could be just in any instance. Therefore, it is my view that chartered banks should continue to be allowed to move across the country without the permission of the government or the Inspector General of Banks, establish branches at their own volition without the permission of any one and move into or out of any province without interference from government.
Many people say the government should have the right to interfere. Mr. Speaker, government influence is far from benign. We have seen examples of government influence which has been wrong, punitive and damaging. The history of this country can give many illustrations. Man's motives, when he gets into government and into power, are not necessarily the most pure at all times. Power which rests within government must not, in the type of economy and society which we in Canada want, move into our financial institutions. I do not mind savings and loans associations being organized under the aegis of government. They are like a post office savings bank.
Personally, I would much rather see the Alberta treasury branches brought under the operations of the Bank Act as a private bank-I say private as opposed to being publicly owned by the province. It is only in recent years that the treasury branches have been successful, but they could be more successful given the privileges of a chartered bank. Of course, treasury branches carry on certain activities which are not allowed to chartered banks, and I agree that this is an anomaly.
However, the situation does not justify inserting into the Bank Act, the privilege of allowing governments to invest in existing banks or to participate in the creation of new banks whether by private bill or by letters patent. I have referred to this question generally, because many of the amendments under my name are frankly consequential in a number of sections. These amendments attempt to wipe the slate clean, once and for all, of government being able to enter banking. I oppose amendment No. 5 which is before us. In due course, I will commend to hon. members the amendments which I have put forward and which would eliminate entirely any government interest in any chartered bank. As far as we know, the shares in chartered banks may be owned at the present time by trustees of government pension funds, but not directly because there are disabilities on directors.
Bank Act
No government wants to own shares in a bank unless it can have directors. That is the nature of the beast. It insists that if it is going to put up some money it shall have some say. No one can gainsay that. As a matter of fact, the justification for allowing governments to invest in chartered banks is so that they may appoint directors-so that governments may have a say and influence on the direction of their affairs. I do not think that is what we want in Canada, and I would so move.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this amendment. I have the highest regard for the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), for his knowledge of banking and so on, but there are one or two points which I think are relevant.
First of all, I believe that a government, whether federal, provincial or municipal, has a responsibility to reflect in its policies the thinking of the people who elected it. If some time in the future the people of a province were to elect a government with a very definite mandate to get into the banking business, that government would be unable to do so because of the laws passed here. In my view that is not a democratic procedure.
1 should also like to speak to the question of freedom of choice. I think governments should have some freedom of choice also. While there is much to be said on both sides, I feel that a strict mandate prohibiting a provincial government, for instance, from going into the banking business really amounts to the federal government telling the provinces what is or is not good for them. Provincial governments should be able to carry out the dictates of the people who elected them and not have to do what a senior government says they can or cannot do. I do not agree with this omnipotence of the federal government. I think the people are omnipotent.
If the people of a province are so dissatisfied with the chartered banking system that they ask the provincial government to go into the banking business in competition, I do not see anything wrong with that. It would be acting as a government, not just looking into people's records. There is much to be said for the remarks of the hon. member regarding directors.
I should like to mention one or two points which make me suspicious of the provision that provincial governments cannot enter the banking business under any circumstances-whether 95 per cent of the people of a province wants it to establish a bank in competition or not. That cannot be done-because an act of the federal government says it cannot be done. I do not like that type of procedure, Mr. Speaker. Surely a provincial government should be in a position to carry out the wishes of the people who elected it. It should not be subject to some other power telling it that it cannot take such action.
I remember the early depression years in Alberta, in 1935- I was not a member of the legislature at that time. The government of the day was elected on a very anti-bank feeling. The people were very unhappy with the banks because during the depression years they withdrew credit right and left. Many

November 12, 1980
Bank Act
companies were put into bankruptcy and, as we used to say, there was hunger in the midst of plenty.
Those banks were not operating in accordance with the wishes of the people and so the people were unhappy. The result was almost a landslide victory for the party that proposed to change the banking system but, unfortunately, it could not get a charter from the federal government to form a bank. Instead, it formed what were known as the treasury branches. The reason it wanted a bank was that it could have the privilege of arranging for the expansion of credit, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton West. If you hold so many dollars in the Bank of Canada you can expand that and lend, I believe, up to 14 times the amount. This gives the bank tremendous avenue for making money or for service, whichever way you want to look at it.
The treasury branches could not do that, however. They could not lend the money of the depositers under the provisions contained in the Bank Act of that time. Each customer had to sign a statement giving permission to lend their money and so the treasury branch came into being. It is a pretty profitable institution today.
Had the treasury branches been subject to the provisions of the Bank Act, however, then last year the provincial government of Alberta would not have been able to offer the tremendous benefits of reduced interest to the farmers and the developers of that province.
Sometimes people wonder why industry has prospered in Alberta. One reason is that the provincial government provided for loans to be available from the treasury branches and not at an exorbitant rate of interest. They had the freedom to do that because they did not have to abide by any rules set out by the Bank of Canada as did the chartered banks. As a result, many people left the chartered banks and went to the treasury branches.
To tell someone that they cannot form a bank is to do things by the backdoor. Had the treasury branches been formed in the same way as a chartered bank there would have been
advantages and disadvantages. They would have come under the rules that apply to all other banks but they would have been able to expand their credit. Today, that expansion of credit could be a tremendous thing for any province or any country.
We have to look carefully at exactly at what we are trying to accomplish, Mr. Speaker. What harm would there be if the province of Ontario wanted to establish a bank in competition with the other banks? We say we want competition, so would it not be just as well for the people of Ontario, through their government, to form, say, the Bank of Ontario, and then expand credit in the interest of all of the people of the province instead of just those who happen to be the shareholders of a bank?
Let me give an illustration, Mr. Speaker-this is not in the banking field but it is something similar. During the depression years premiums for fire insurance on homes in Alberta became exorbitant. Hundreds of people could not take out insurance, as a result. The government of the day was not socialist but it offered to form an insurance company in competition with the other insurance companies because it thought it could be done at a reduced rate. It was done, and the Alberta Insurance Office came into being. It was swamped with hundreds of thousands of applications. It did so well that all the insurance companies had to reduce their rates in order to stay in business. It was competitive, Mr. Speaker.

Except as provided in sections 4 and 5, the price per net clean cubic metre of crude oil having a density at 15dC of eight hundred fifteen kilograms per cubic metre or less, and containing less that one gram of sulphur per kilogram, shall not be more than $108.75 as at the Edmonton, Alberta, terminal of Interprovincial Pipe Line Limited and the prices of all crude oil that were derived or were derivable from or related to the price of the said crude oil prior to the making of these Regulations shall continue to be derived from or related to the price of that crude oil according to the practices of the trade prevailing immediately prior to the making of these Regulations, including practices related to the establishment of differences in price on account of variances in density, sulphur content, location and the establishment of prices for mixed streams of crude oil except that, where in any month after the making of these Regulations, a gathering charge or transportation toll applicable to any particular kind or quality of crude oil to which this section applies, is established or amended, the gathering charge or transportation toll as established or amended shall be added to the maximum price for that quality or kind of crude oil or shall be substituted for the charge or toll applicable to that quality or kind of crude oil immediately prior to the making of these Regulations, when calculating the maximum price for that quality or kind of crude oil.
4.	The price for natural gasoline or condensate per net clean cubic metre shall not be more thatn $115.05 as at the Edmonton, Alberta, terminal of Interprovincial Pipe Line Limited.
5.	The price for any hydrocarbon or mixture of hydrocarbons per net clean cubic metre that is produced by extraction from oil sands and is not a refinery oil product within the meaning of section 26 of the National Energy Board Part VI Regulations shall not be more than $111.90 as at the Edmonton, Alberta, terminal of Interprovincial Pipe Line Limited, excluding any compensation paid or payable in respect of any
such hydrocarbon or mixture of hydrocarbons pursuant to Part IV of the Petroleum Administration Act.
6.	The maximum price per net clean cubic metre for any crude oil not specified in section 3, 4 or 5 or derivable from section 3 shall not be more than $115.25 at the point of sale before its transmission or transportation out of the province in which it was produced, extracted or recovered, less any gathering charge or transportation toll from that point of sale to Montreal.
